Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has raised several matters. I find his reference to correspondence with my office shocking and disturbing, because I have a rule that correspondence must be answered within ten days. I have already sent off an inquiry to find out what is involved in the situation to which he refers.
The hon. member also said that in any relocation scheme environmental and ecological considerations must be taken into account. I agree with him. As the legislation provides, before the CTC can act an urban development plan must be laid before it, and I find it inconceivable that any such plan would be drawn up without taking into account the ecological and environmental aspects of the proposed relocation scheme.
The hon. member was also concerned about the application process and the cost sharing formula. He will note from Part I of the bill that any relocation or rerouting proposal will require the closest degree of intergovernmental consultation and co-operation. As we see it, the urban development plan and the transportation plan will be drawn up at the initiation of the municipality or province involved. It will be referred to the CTC with comments on any federal programs that my ministry is involved in to ensure co-ordination, and the Department of Transport will concern itself with the transportation aspects of any relocation. I think in this legislation we have tried to provide for good interdepartmental and intergovernmental consultation and co-ordination.
The hon. member referred to the Canadian Transport Commission. Their role is provided for in the legislation for obvious reasons: they are the regulatory agency at the federal level with jurisdiction over railroads, railroad rights of way and railroad activities. I think the hon. member will agree that it would have been wrong to set up another federal regulatory body to deal solely with railroad relocation.
I agree with the hon. member on the point he and a number of other members raised, namely that the municipalities, the provinces, members of parliament and the government are entitled to expect the CTC to operate

efficiently and effectively and with speed when dealing with applications. Several hon. members have said that the CTC needs a good shaking up. I believe we are entitled to expect it to deal with applications made under Part I in an effective and an efficient manner, and I think the Minister of Transport can be relied upon to ensure that this will be done.
With regard to questions of safety, I would refer hon. members to Part II and III of the bill. Part II provides for special expenses for grade crossings and grade separation schemes, and Part III provides for amendments to the grade crossing fund, doubling-and I am speaking loosely-the federal contributions to grade crossings and grade separations.
The removal of grade crossings has made an important contribution to safety. Statistics show that while automobile accidents have increased over the last few years, the percentage of automobile accidents at grade crossings has decreased. This is largely the result of safety work at level crossings and also the large numbers of grade separations that have been constructed.
The amendments to Parts II and III, which allow the CTC and the grade crossing fund to work on a great many more safety features at level crossings by way of safety devices, also allow for the building of more grade separations, and thus make an important contribution to safety.
I am not familiar with the case referred to by the hon. member as I am not responsible for the grade crossing fund, but I will give instructions that this be looked into. I do not understand why action was not taken because there was only one track and not two.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I cannot say what the particular plans are for Hamilton under this legislation, but knowing the leadership of that city and the representation it has in this House I am sure the case will be put very effectively and vigorously before the CTC. Indeed, if we are not very careful Hamilton will manage to get the bulk of any moneys provided under this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, just before clause 5 carries, I should like to stress once again the purport of the remarks I was making earlier on this whole question of relocation of rail lines. The minister has failed as yet to comment on the question of the Vancouver harbour, and the proposed relocation of some of the rail lines connected with it as well as the financial plans that have been brought forward from time to time. Will these plans have to be reshaped or redrawn by the National Harbours Board? Would a government agency be responsible for this? Would the municipality of the city of Vancouver or the province be the one to do it? The minister has failed to deal with these questions.
I should like to quote from an article by Mr. Mark Wilson of January 9, 1974 concerning these problems. The article is headed "Roundtrip over Burrard Inlet takes 14 days". That seems like an unusually long journey for a boxcar. The article goes on to say:
We are just not adapted to moving a car from say North Vancouver to Marpole. Besides, 95 per cent of the traffic coming from the North Shore is moving east like the potash, coal and sulphur trains returning empty to Alberta or Saskatchewan.
Then, further we find this:
CP Rail says the CNR service poses a problem, but it looks for long-term relief to the eventual relocation of North Shore bulk loading facilities at Roberts Bank.
The article goes on to suggest that there should be a great deal of relocation of trackage in that Vancouver area. Is the government aware of the existing change of the plan for the Vancouver area surrounding Burrard Inlet? There is a suggestion made with regard to the location of a new CNR marshalling yard which would do away with the Burlington Northern Railway marshalling yards. Surely the minister, who represents the city of Vancouver, could advise us whether or not there is an over-all plan now either by the National Harbours Board or the city of Vancouver that would follow up this relocation of tracks in and around that harbour.
I cannot see for the life of me why we should be forced to use an American marshalling yard. In fact the CNR uses two marshalling yards, one a great distance out of the city of Vancouver and the other the Burlington Northern. The CPR really uses a small marshalling yard near the Alberta wheat pool operation and one at the end of Moody Bay. I do not know why we cannot have a greater amount of cohesion in respect of traffic. I do not suggest that there should be a terminal railway company operating at the port, but I suggest there should be a greater relocation of trackage to facilitate the movement of boxcars in and out of that terminal which would assist in the movement of grain as well as, of container cars. I am sure the minister and his department could investigate to see what is being done with regard to an over-all plan for that harbour. There was a study in 1969. I am wondering whether it is still around or whether it is necessary to have another study made.
I see it is five o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

Speech:
Mr. Chairman, while we are dealing with this particular clause I must say I am very pleased the minister has accepted the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Scarborough West. As I study the provisions in this bill, I must say I find it very difficult to pass judgment on this piece of legislation before knowing what the overall transportation policy of the government is going to be.
I share the concern expressed by other hon. members about the very wide powers the CTC is being granted, powers which in my opinion go well beyond the matter of regulation. This was alluded to by the minister in previous discussion.
It is very difficult to know whether to take seriously some of the statements by government spokesmen which suggest that inter-city transport, particularly in high density areas, will revert to a large degree to rail transportation. That strikes at the very heart of this bill.
What concerns me even more is the procedure with regard to appeal provisions. I wonder if the minister can explain whether section 64 of the National Transportation Act, which gives the governor in council the power, at any time at his discretion, or upon petition of any party, person or company, to alter, vary or rescind any order or decision that has been proposed by the CTC, would apply to the provisions of this particular bill. I think that section is very important, particularly when we consider the vacuum in the entire transportation policy throughout the

various modes of transportation in this country, especially in the field of urban transportation.
I do not think any area of transportation is more important at this time, as far as the future of transportation is concerned, than urban transportation. It is quite clear to many members that we probably stand on the threshold of many new, innovative and technological concepts in the field of inter-city and urban rapid transportation. We hear talk of 300 miles per hour trains in high density areas such as Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal, magnetic levitation trains.
We hear of the importance of surface transportation by rail as being something of very major importance in respect to fuel economy, having regard to the energy situation. It seems that at this time we are granting a tremendous amount of authority to a body, which is largely a regulatory body, to pass judgment on the future development of our transportation network in this very critical area. I believe there is a great future in surface transportation, particularly inter-city rail transportation.
At the moment we find the government spending huge sums to develop STOL aircraft for inter-city travel. We shall have to make up our minds soon whether to develop an efficient surface transportation network, or whether to rely on the STOL transportation system. The minister has often suggested that the CTC is an all-powerful body over which he has no control, save in exceptional circumstances, and we still do not know what those circumstances are. I am wondering whether section 64 of the National Transportation Act which set up the CTC would apply in this case, whether there is a right of appeal and, if so, what is the proper appeal procedure to be followed.
We know that the CTC has moved very slowly in implementing some of the sections of that act. I need only mention the famous rapeseed case which was brought to the attention of the commission in 1970 and with respect to which a decision is still awaited. It was demonstrated to the commission that the freight rate being charged was inequitable and prejudicial to the public interest. Yet after four years this case has still to be resolved.
Surely when we embark on legislation which is so important to the development of effective urban transportation, these questions should be settled before the legislation is allowed to pass. The bill is basically a good one and the government is to be commended for presenting it, but there are areas which need to be clarified and there is no better time to do so than the present. Having served on the transport committee for some time and having heard both the President of the CTC and the Minister of Transport give evidence before that committee, it is my impression we still cannot form any clear picture of the relationship.
The minister suggests the CTC is holding him up and preventing him from doing things he wants to do. The CTC, on the other hand, says there are matters of policy involved and that it has no control over policy considerations. In any case, I feel that adequate appeal procedures should be established, and if the minister can tell us what mechanism can be used for this purpose he would be doing the committee a service by clarifying an important part of the bill.
April 30, 1974

Surely, the minister knows that profits are a cyclical phenomena and that establishing a customary profit margin for a product based on the last decade may not be an easy task. In fact, it may be impossible.
If you base your measure of customary profit margin for a firm on last year's performance, for example, it would not be appropriate for every industry. Some were depressed while some were having a bumper year. Therefore, this government will only be increasing an already large bureaucracy, and God only knows what the result will be. The Food Prices Review Board is a good example. When the Food Prices Review Board was set up on May 28, 1973, its initial budget was $500,000 and its permanent staff numbered about 20. Since then its budget has quadrupled to the point where it is almost $2 million and its staff has more than doubled to 48. In addition, the Food Prices Review Board has entered into 29 contracts for 31 studies, thereby further increasing its bureaucracy.

Let us take a look at the power of this bill. The cabinet is given the ultimate decision as to what action to take with respect to demanding payment from suppliers or price roll backs and freezes under this bill. It may, on its own initiative, declare an emergency situation and refer the pricing policy of a particular supplier to the Trade Practices Commission.
Again on its own initiative, it may order the supplier to pay the Crown what it has decided are undue profits. In my view, that constitutes an arbitrary imposition of tax without reference to a ways and means motion of this House. I hope the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) will have an opportunity to say more about that later.
In order for the cabinet and/or the proposed Trade Practices Commission to exercise the discretionary powers under this bill, it will be necessary to closely monitor the market place. The minister may say that this role will be carried out by the Food Prices Review Board. I see the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), a distinguished member of the food prices committee, smiling because he is skeptical. He knows whereof I speak. If we had to depend on the Food Prices Review Board to do the monitoring necessary under this bill, I would tell the House that this speaks for itself. Furthermore, the process by which this bill would become operative could be a long and cumbersome one which would considerably diminish its effectiveness.
Editorial writers and columnists all across the country have either dismissed the bill as so much political puffery, which it is, or have described it as bad law, which it is, that should never find its way as presented into the statute books of this country. The bill is imprecise in its application and vague in its definition. We have a responsibility to all our constituents. It would hang like a sword over every business person in the country because it could be selectively applied at any time. In the words of today's lead editorial in the Globe and Mail "There would be no fair warning". After the contribution by the minister today, he would do well to sit and ponder what he has produced before this House.

Speech:
That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we Canadians today have reached a threshold of great challenge and great opportunity.
We are thriving as seldom before in our history. Our growth of output, employment and real income surpasses that of virtually every other industrial country.
But we are confronted by the scourge of inflation, worldwide in its origins and impact. No other issue more deeply disturbs our country, this government or me, as Minister of Finance. While we have suffered less from inflation than most other nations, we can and must do better to overcome it and alleviate its burdens.
The challenge facing the country is to break the inflationary spiral. But we must do this in ways that will not erode our prosperity nor damage our growth. Let no one think that this can be done easily or quickly. It will take time and effort. And until we have brought inflation under control, it is imperative that the burdens it inflicts be equitably shared and that those people who are most vulnerable be decently protected.
An opportunity is at hand to strengthen the Canadian economy and to improve the standard of living of every Canadian. This will require the wise development of our unique storehouse of resources-both material and human. In doing this, we must not allow ourselves to be diverted by ill-considered and illusory policies that would prejudice our long-term interests as a nation.
This budget has three main purposes. The first is to reinforce our attack on inflation through encouraging increased supplies of goods and services. This we will do by maintaining the strong expansion of the economy and by increasing the productive capacity of our farms, fisheries and industries. The second is to act directly against high prices where that is practical. The third is further to alleviate the adverse impact of rising prices on all Canadians, particularly those with lower incomes.

International Developments
The problem of inflation is clearly world-wide in origin. The Economic Review that I tabled last week deals with this at some length, and documents the leading role which accelerating international prices have played in our domestic price experience. Indeed, world inflation can be traced to the enormous buildup in international liquidity associated with the massive deficits in the U.S. balance of payments which ultimately resulted in the breakdown of the Bretton Woods exchange rate system. More recently, the concurrence of economic expansion in most industrial countries, coupled with major crop failures, led to an explosion of commodity and food prices. Last December, the world was hit further by a cutback in the supply of oil and staggering increases in its price. With so many nations facing massive shocks to their international balances, the world community is threatened by fragmentation and protectionism.
May 6, 1974

These developments constitute a menace to all countries, and not least to Canada, given our dependence on international trade and investment. No country can long prosper in a world of unsettled international financial and trade arrangements. This is clearly a time for renewed co-operation and strenuous efforts by all countries to rebuild a viable international trade and payments system. Let me stress that Canada has been playing a full role in the broad international effort to achieve this objective.
This government came early to the conclusion that under the conditions of great uncertainty emerging in the world, floating exchange rates were appropriate. Indeed, Canada adopted this policy four years ago. This approach has now been widely adopted and seems in these troubled times to be serving us all well.
In the pursuit of international monetary reform, Canada has persistently urged that the discussions should concentrate on matters of immediate importance where progress is possible. Last January, this approach of making progress where we could was endorsed by world finance ministers at their meetings in Rome.
Canada has also urged, and will continue to urge, that the International Monetary Fund, the key international financial institution, be strengthened in order to play an increasing role in maintaining world monetary order. We support the proposal for a new council of the IMF, composed of ministers, to meet frequently to tackle directly the major international financial issues, especially world inflation.
On the trade side, we have been concerned, as the energy crisis emerged, that countries might individually take restrictive action to relieve their balance of payments deficits. I have stressed this danger at many international meetings. I therefore welcome and support the efforts being made in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, and in the work begun at the Washington Energy Conference, to ensure that countries avoid beggar-thy-neighbour policies. Speech:
One hon. member said that they have just returned. They have returned while yet the light holds forth and burns. It is interesting to note the attitude taken in the last few weeks by some great American papers toward the parliamentary system. They pay the system great tribute. I will not quote because my time is limited. They said, in so many words, that so long as the representatives of the Crown live true to their oaths of office, there cannot be a Watergate in Canada. That was a tremendous tribute to our parliamentary system. The Americans, in attempting to get away from the British parliamentary system, made the president an all powerful king who might believe, as some of his predecessors did, that he is above the law.
In successive amendments to the rules of this House we have lost control of a basic right which is fundamental to parliament-the right to the fullest examination of expenditures. Today there is no such right. Despite all the gyrationS'-we witnessed this afternoon, one cannot get around the situation that there are estimates unpassed from the previous parliament. The first thing we must do is this: we must return to this House, as a committee of the whole, the right to examine ministers on their shortcomings and on their achievements.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, it is not without a considerable degree of trepidation that I, as a freshman member of this House, rise to make my first remarks in this chamber in the course of this crucial debate with respect to the west coast grain handlers' dispute.
As the representative of Assiniboia constituency-one of this nation's greatest agricultural and, particularly, grain producing regions-this dispute and its settlement are of paramount concern to me at the moment. It is essential that the interruption in Vancouver grain movement be brought now to a speedy conclusion by parliament because it is quite apparent that exhaustive efforts- they have been exhaustive on all sides-toward a negotiated solution have not been, and will not be, successful.
I regret-as I am sure most hon. members of this House regret-the fact that we are here today dealing with this problem in this manner. Surely the floor of this House must not become the commonplace location for major labour-management negotiations in this country to take place. The prime responsibility in this area, through the collective bargaining process, rests-and ought to rest- with employers and employees. Under our laws, and in the national interest in most cases, they are quite properly called upon to sit down together to resolve their differences, find common ground and reach contract settlements without damaging slowdowns or destructive work stoppages, and without possible mischief or violence and the eventual necessity of parliamentary intervention. But in the present circumstances, parliament has no alternative but to take this action, and I hope expeditiously, to conclude a contract so that our grain exports through Vancouver can resume.
October 7, 1974

I must say that I appreciate the view expressed by the spokesman for the New Democratic Party, that his party wants this legislation to move forward quickly so that grain can begin to move through Vancouver. I regret the attitude of the official opposition, which seems not to be very concerned about the situation at the moment.
I suppose somewhere in the annals of our industrial history we might find what could be described as examples of perfect negotiations or perfect industrial relations. But most surely these examples would be few and far between in our less than perfect world. The present situation in Vancouver falls far short of perfection when viewed from almost any perspective, and the difficulties of this past summer have taken place against a sorry background of sour relationships and discord extending back more than a decade. In view of this sad history, I particularly welcome the proposal today by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) that an industrial inquiry commission will soon be appointed to thoroughly investigate the history of labour relations in the grain handling industry at Vancouver.
Requests for such a move have come from such diverse sources as the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association and, I believe, the National Farmers' Union. I know we will all wish the commission well in its work toward achieving a better industrial relationship between the grain handling companies and their employees. I am sure prairie grain producers are looking forward to an era of more stability in this field so that they need not fear further costly disruptions in the movement of their grain into export position.
There are two general issues with which I shall deal briefly. First, some parties in this House and outside have tried to paint the government as the ogre in this sad situation. I ask members, before they make their judgment in this case, to look carefully at the chronology of events which stretch back for one year. Negotiations began for a new contract on October 19, 1973, almost a full year ago. The existing contract was due to expire on November 30. Direct negotiations between the parties continued for almost two months, without success.
The parties requested federal mediation assistance about the middle of December, 1973. That assistance was forthcoming immediately and two skilled mediators struggled to find reasonable common ground for agreement between the parties. They worked for another two months but were unable to show signs of progress. A clear impasse had been reached and the Minister of Labour moved to appoint as conciliation commissioner Dr. Perry, who began his duties on February 15, 1974, four full months after discussions had begun originally. So this was hardly a premature move.
The appointment apparently was well received. Dr. Perry is a skilled man, an expert who is widely respected and well known in the field and, as the minister pointed out earlier, he had worked with these same parties a few years previously. It is interesting to note that amid all the controversy surrounding the dispute nobody has attacked Dr. Perry's competence, ability or impartiality. There has been criticism from some sides of the recommendations he

put forward, yet nobody has attacked his ability to deal with the situation or his competence in the field. Dr. Perry worked with both sides for 214 months but was unable to draw them together. Finally, he produced a report recommending what he saw to be a fair and reasonable settlement.

I quote as follows from the preamble to Dr. Perry's report:
-the recommendations which follow can hardly be expected to do more than indicate a series of intermediate changes with which both parties may be able to associate themselves as they try to conclude a settlement in a difficult year.
The Perry report does not discuss the basic issues at all. They are productivity, efficiency and incentives. The real issue is not to do something that will add to the inflationary pressure in the country, but to do something that will move more grain through export positions at the lowest possible cost per bushel. With trains and ships operating around the clock, seven days a week, steps must be taken to put grain terminals on the same basis. It is obvious, too, that we must move toward a system whereby clean, ready to export grain is moved to export positions.
I am certain of one thing: we will not get increased productivity by parliament legislating this settlement. On May 23, 1974, the government took action under section 181 to make a strike or lock-out illegal until after the election. There is doubt about the legality of the government's action, and the sloppy staff work showed up when they omitted from the order the terminal owned by James Richardson. The title of Bill C-12 is "An act to provide for the resumption of grain handling operations on the west coast of Canada". I would like the House to understand that two terminals one operated by the Alberta Wheat Pool in Victoria and a terminal in Prince Rupert have operated throughout the Vancouver shut-down.
Ministers of the Crown made it clear that unless the parties in the meantime reached agreement, a settlement would be legislated in accordance with the commissioner's recommendations. Any chance of effective and meaningful bargaining ended absolutely when the Minister of Labour said during the election campaign that the government would, if re-elected, legislate implementation of the report. This promise was reiterated later by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. There remained a great-deal of ground for negotiation.
On August 1, 1974, the government of Canada made two rather dramatic moves in the grain business. They granted the companies an unprecedented increase in the tariff for both country elevator operation and for terminal operation. This increase was granted by order in council P C. 1974-1702, dated July 30, 1974, to be effective August 1, 1974. At the same time, the government reduced the payment for number one bread wheat to the western farmer from $3.75 to $2.25 a bushel, a reduction of some 40 per cent. On August 8, the no strike, no lock-out order expired. On August 23, 1974, strikes plus lock-outs, completely shut down the Vancouver grain terminals. The greatest grain exporting port in a hungry world sat idle. Works for the general advantage indeed!

October 8, 1974
Grain Handlers' Strike
Instead of reminding the grain companies of their responsibilities, I suggest this government should have looked to their own responsibilities in this matter. It must be obvious even to this government that third party intervention is necessary in labour disputes right from the start, and I do not necessarily mean government intervention. In the case before us, I suggest three or four farmers sitting in as observers would have tended to keep both parties on the track.
History tells us that almost every time the government interferes with agriculture, they spoil the market; and if the marketing is wrong, we might as well plow under all the other effort. The expansion of our grain exports and competitive strength depend more on our own efforts than on our reliance on negotiating with other countries. There are a number of actions and policies we can initiate unilaterally which will contribute to our goals of increased trade.
Our greatest need is to have a consistently dependable supply of major grain items, at competitive world prices, at seaboard. Instead, heavy-handed interference by ministers of the Crown has resulted in the present impasse. If the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board wants to nationalize the grain industry, and this is a first step, he should be honest enough to say so. I quote as follows from the Alberta Wheat Pool publication "Budget" of October 4, 1974:
G. L. Harrold, president, Alberta Wheat Pool, said in Calgary recently that a statement by labour minister, John Munro threatening nationalization of the grain handling industry is out of order and ill-timed. Madam Speaker, the matter I bring to the adjournment debate this evening is one of mounting urgency and importance. I thank the minister for the tone of his reply when I asked him yesterday if he had been able to find the additional $2.5 million for the Medical Research Council since his undertaking to try to do so earlier this year. However, I also want to say how profoundly disappointed I was with the content of his response, that he had not been successful in his efforts.
The amount we are talking about, $2.5 million, is not large when one considers that the departments' overall budget is almost $5 billion. However, it is an extremely critical amount, not only to our scientific community but in determining the future standard of health care for all Canadians.
Earlier this year there was considerable discussion in committee and testimony provided by expert witnesses to substantiate the crying need for additional funding in medical research. At that time it was stated, and I quote:
Since a nation's health is basic to its economy, biomedical science policies should be the concern of every Canadian. The presence of a crisis in a small area of government concern which may have a very large effect on our nation should be recognized now before matters go beyond a state of repair.
The plea was made to abandon the on-again, off-again style of nourishing research in Canada. Economists are agreed that any viable industry spends about 4.5 per cent on basic and marketing research. The biomedical sciences are not even asking for 2 per cent of its industry's budget. They are pleading against further erosion.
The government's decision to grant only a small increase in last year's budget to MRC and subsequently to hold the line on this year's figure has not only deprived medical research of a realistic increase in funds, but as well subjected existing funds to serious erosion by twodigit inflation. The situation was deemed critical by many concerned Canadians last spring, and the intervening months have seen a continuing deterioration.
In June a joint statement was issued by the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation, the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies and the Association of Canadian Medical Colleges which pointed out, and I quote:
In some medical schools, research programs in clinical departments are shrinking or closing down entirely because, in the absence of council support, they have no source of funds. Potential researchers are discouraged from entering upon a research career and the continuance of research activities by existing medical scientists is threatened.
Since then numerous representations have been made to me pointing out that certain projects are grinding to a halt because mounting inflation makes it impossible to absorb increased costs from funds made available even earlier this year.

October 8, 1974
Adjournment Debate
Recently the Medical Research Council announced that it does not have adequate funds to support the project of a computerized pancreas, a project which has potential benefit for thousands of Canadian diabetics.
The greatest potential for disaster in the government's niggardly commitment to medical research is its impact on young graduates contemplating research careers. Last year only one per cent of the graduating class in one of our leading medical schools planned to enter a career in biomedical research and teaching, as compared with 10 per cent as recently as 1969. The appalling attrition in recruitment for medical research is understandable, given the vulnerability of the future of medical research, but it can have disastrous consequences for future generations of Canadians.
I plead with the minister and his colleagues to remove the constraints which were placed on medical research earlier this year, and to ensure that future budgets will include a constant dollar application and a realistic and guaranteed percentage of total health costs for research.

In the throne speech the government has said, as it has said many times in the past, that higher production will be the way we will achieve, if not lower prices or stable prices, at least, as the speech puts it, "the slowing down of price advances." But this can be so only if an increased supply of goods is allowed by the government to exert downward pressures on prices. Increasing the supply of goods and services will do little, if anything, to lower prices if suppliers, because of their economic power, can keep their prices at the same level or even increase them. Increasing supply will not bring about lower prices if government policy itself serves to maintain prices, even when supply increases, or if government policy ratchets them even higher with each increase in the level of supply.
The American economist, Henrik Houthaker, has proposed an urgent examination of all his federal government's regulations and programs to see if they are in fact helping keep prices up. We should carry out this kind of review in our country and the government should take action, in light of it, on an urgent basis.
Speaking about this kind of approach, another American economist, Gardner Ackley, has said that "this means a concerted attack on structural rigidities in our economy and an energetic effort to dismantle the many institutional, largely governmental, arrangements which raise particular costs and prices." As I said earlier in my remarks, we must make efforts to remove structural rigidities that contribute to inflation. The increasing of flexibility and of competitive pressures in our economy is a key micro-economic way of dealing with our inflation problems. The Farm Improvement Loans Act and Small Businesses Loans Act have been in effect for many years, and I am sure that members are reasonably familiar with them. They will recall that last spring the acts were amended following a full review by the government in order to expand their scope and increase their effectiveness and usefulness to borrowers.
These acts have played a useful role in meeting the credit requirements of a large number of Canadians. The Farm Improvement Loans Act has been particularly important as a source of intermediate credit to farmers. Up to the end of June this year, loans extended under FILA totalled over $3 billion, so I think that contradicts what my hon. friend has said. In fact it has been found useful. Such loans reached a record of $230 million in 1973.
Since inception of the Small Businesses Loans program over $300 million was lent to June, 1974. This is another indicator that it is being used. Lending under this program has been rising sharply in recent years, and was over $30 million in 1973.
In the first six months of this year lending under these programs declined. I think that is what my hon. friend is endeavouring to highlight. This may well have been due to a reluctance by lenders to participate in the programs because of a growing differential between the rates they were permitted to charge at that time and commercial rates of interest. In this respect, hon. members may be aware that the permissible rates are determined twice a year, on April 1 and October 1, on the basis of a formula contained in regulations. The formula rate is the average yield on government of Canada bonds during the six months preceding the rate change, plus 1 per cent.
It will be noted that, due to the averaging period, the formula rate will lag behind current commercial rates when the latter are changing rapidly. This lag became significant in the first part of 1974 when the bank prime rate moved from 91/2 per cent in January to 11 'h per cent in July. During this period the rate for the vast majority of these guaranteed loans, all except those for the purchase of land under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, was 8 'A per cent until March, and dropped to 8 per cent on April 1. Thus the formula rate became increasingly out of line with rates charged by lenders on regular loans, and by July the negative differential had become quite significant.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I am always overwhelmed by the multitude of my colleagues who listen to my voice at this hour. On the other hand, to those who are not staying I feel like Lady MacBeth who said: "Stand not on the order of your going".
Last Tuesday's question to the minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), concerning the Geneva Conference and the role of the Palestine Liberation Organization at that gathering was prompted by my continued interest and profound concern for the future of the Palestinian people.
There are many blunders, many failures, many moral wrongs in our age as in all preceding ages, but I believe nothing is a greater affront to our conscience than the Palestinian refugee question which has been a blight upon our record for the past quarter century. One and one-half million people driven from their homes or fleeing them in fear have languished in tents and shacks for 28 years. Discouragement, disillusionment is their lot. Children have grown to manhood knowing no home, knowing no hope. Not surprisingly in this life so degrading to the human personality disillusionment has turned to despair, and frustration to desperation. Not surprisingly the refugees ask: does any one care; will no one take up our cause?
The Arab inhabitants of Palestine were not consulted and, I fear, not considered when others decided that a new state of Israel should be set up in Palestine. I cannot here tonight discuss the violence and terror which went on in Palestine over the years prior to the carving out of the Republic of Israel-violence not by any means confined to the Arabs, or shall we say, the Palestinians.
But suffice to say there has been a painful, cruel lack of concern for the host of huddled refugees in the far-flung camps of the Middle East. UNRA has dispensed funds, but nothing like a decent lifestyle has been established, even if we set aside the vital question of the right of these people to a home of their own rather than a half-way hostel on a road which seems never to open up. Only in recent years has there been some recognition of the intensity and importance of the fate and status of the Palestinian refugees.
In this session of the General Assembly of the United Nations a recent decision was made to take up the general issue as a separate item for plenary discussion. The other day It was decided to hear a spokesman of the Palestine Liberation Organization at that great international organization in New York.
I regret that Canada found itself unwilling to join the vast majority of delegations prepared to hear a spokesman for the long suffering Palestinians. We took the familiar safety device of abstention. Of course there are problems, but there is a difference in this case. There is an interesting difference between our performance at ICAO or UNESCO. We know there are problems. All but one of the Arab states now seem prepared to look upon the PLO as

the spokesman for the Palestinians and all present voted in favour.
The government of Jordan has a different point of view from the rest of the Arab states. Does Canada agree with the Jordanian position? Canada is in the Middle East in the UNEF. Canada is a charter member of the United Nations. I believe we are wisely establishing new diplomatic missions in Arab states. Having long recommended such a move, I expressed pleasure on the opening of an embassy in Saudi Arabia. I am glad that Yemen is strengthening its diplomatic contacts with us. The appointment of an ambassador from Canada, stationed in Baghdad, is long overdue.
But what I should like to know is the view of the government on the situation referred to in my question, and I hope that the distinguished parliamentary secretary, my long time friend from New Brunswick, will tell us tonight what is the view of the government of Canada. What are we doing to make our contribution toward peace in the troubled Middle East? Let us never forget that Armageddon is located in that part of the world. How are we demonstrating our awareness of the new prospects for advancing the cause and the lot of the long suffering Palestinians? Such a tragic situation, so egregious an affront to human dignity, cannot go on forever; indeed it should not go on longer.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the question by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) on October 8, let me begin, as he did, by referring to the community employment strategy, which is a long-term plan, as he indicated, to combat the problems of the chronically unemployed or under-employed.
The hon. member expanded on the terms of reference of the original question and referred in a broad sense to government policies. It is impossible in three minutes to speak of the impact of DREE on the Atlantic Region, although, without question, DREE has been successful in creating many jobs. Tonight I can only speak on behalf of the Department of Manpower.
Let me begin by talking of the community employment strategy which is aimed at helping specific groups which experience particular difficulty in keeping and finding regular employment. Some of these are the physically handicapped, the mentally retarded, socially handicapped,
ex-inmates of mental or correctional institutions, people living in areas of chronic unemployment, and single parents. In the Atlantic area we know particularly of those in the second last category, people living in areas of chronic unemployment.
This program is being developed in conjunction with National Health and Welfare. Indeed, it is as a result of the policy paper the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) put out last year. One important aspect of it is that it attempts to involve the community in the definition and, indeed, the resolution of their specific problem. To my mind, that is a departure from what we have been doing up until this time. It will tell the community of the impact of our present programs on them and, together with them, try to seek answers to improve those programs and the employment situation in a particular community.
This is a long-range plan. It is one worth undertaking. It will have beneficial effects. However, it in no way indicates that there is any lack of appreciation or emphasis on our present programs or ongoing activities. We want to emphasize the extensive efforts that have already been made by Canada Manpower to reduce unemployment.
The hon. member referred to the Canada Manpower training program. He called into question its effects. I believe that program is certainly worthwhile. The hon. member will agree that in this time of rapid change it is very important that we keep our skilled people up to date. Canadian workers change jobs many times during their careers. It is incumbent upon us to provide continuously educational opportunities for them as they do this.
The $2 billion spent on training programs in the past represents a very successful investment. We have reorganized Manpower Placement Services. I can tell the hon. member that in my own area of Atlantic Canada, for example in my constituency, there has been a decentralization of Manpower services over the past year or 18 months. In my opinion this is of great benefit in meeting the local placement needs.
The department instituted a system of farm labour pools which was designed to ensure that crop harvests are not hindered by inadequate labour supplies.
The hon. member also referred to the short-term job creation program that had been recognized nationally, the local initiatives program. There is certainly agreement that LIP is not the answer to long-term unemployment. It was not designed for that purpose. It has been continually modified since its inception, and will be continually modified during the progress of this parliament, in consultation with members on both sides of the House. We regard this as important and effective. What I like better is the Local Employment Assistance Program which, I feel, has a longterm effect on many areas of unemployment.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make a few brief remarks in connection with the Federal Business Development Bank. In looking over the bill, I note that in clause 4(2) the following is provided:
The corporation in carrying out its objects shall give particular consideration to the needs of small business enterprises.
I think that is an important consideration. There is a need to finance small business in Canada, particularly in western Canada where we do not have, at least in my own province of Saskatchewan, the large type of corporation. I note no interpretation is given of the term "small business enterprise" and I think it would be valuable if such an interpretation were provided in the bill. I also welcome the provisions in the bill pertaining to the managerial advice that might be given to businesses, in the form of counselling and training. This will be welcomed by small businessmen who do not have access to the kind of information and training that is necessary to properly carry on such business.
The basic effect of this bill is to transfer the functions of the Industrial Development Bank from the Bank of Canada to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, which I look upon with mixed feelings. Generally speaking, I would think that the Bank of Canada would look upon a business loan in a businesslike way, whereas I am concerned about the kind of bureaucratic build-up that is occurring in many of our government departments today. I hope that by putting the Federal Business Development Bank under the portfolio of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce we will not end up with a bureaucratic nightmare.
I also hope that the board will develop a policy and use the facilities of the bank for the general interest of all Canada, and that it will not be used as a means of furthering the interests of one region of Canada as opposed to another. When the IDB came into being a few years ago, it was initially very popular among the business community in my constituency and was welcomed. But in recent times the IDB has been used less and less. In the province of Saskatchewan, people have been turning to the provincial government organization known as SEDCO-the Saskatchewan Economic Development Corporation.
This situation has concerned me somewhat because SEDCO sometimes requires the transfer or sale to it of certain of the capital stock of the corporation it is lending money to, with the result that the government is getting its fingers into the pie. It is not taking such shares as security for the loan but, rather, is taking them as a condition of making the loan, and the government remains one of the owners of the small business concerned.
I suggest that one of the reasons there has been a movement away from the IDB is that a great deal of documentation is required before a loan is approved. This sometimes takes several months, and businessmen are not always in a position to wait several months for a decision. If a businessman is developing a new business, he is not in a position to wait this length of time, in view of the weather conditions in my part of the country. Not only is


Federal Business Development Bank Act
lengthy documentation required, but as my learned friend who spoke before me mentioned, assets are tied up, including one's arms and legs. The IDB requires stringent personal guarantees and there are many other restrictions. Having talked to accountants in my own constituency, I am convinced this is one reason small businessmen have not been using the IDB.
I believe the lending policies of the Federal Business Development Bank should be economical and that the amount of accounting and legal work should be at a minimum. I believe that the requirement for security should not be restrictive. I hope this will prove to be a bank that businessmen will be able to go to and get a decision as to whether a loan will be approved without undue delay, with the result they will know where they stand.
I have nothing further to add except that I am in support of the bill and will follow with interest the progress of this bank, over the years.

Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes to make certain amendments to the Trust Companies Act and the Loan Companies Act. These statutes provide for the incorporation and supervision of federally-incorporated trust companies and mortgage loan companies, respectively.

October 29, 1974
Trust Companies Act
Trust companies raise money from the public by accepting deposits and selling guaranteed investment certificates. Loan companies obtain their funds by the sale of debentures and the acceptance of deposits. For both types of companies the relevant statute places a maximum limit on the funds that can be obtained from the public. At present, this maximum limit is 20 times the company's capital and surplus, which can only be reached with the approval of the minister. The effect of these limits is to require the maintenance of at least a minimum excess of assets over liabilities to the public. This provides a safety margin in the sense that any asset losses can be absorbed first by this excess before any question arises as to the ability of the company to meet its obligations.
The maximum limit on the amount that any trust or loan company may borrow from the public was raised in 1970 from 15 to 20 times a company's capital and surplus. However, because of the rapid expansion being experienced by these companies, a number of them are now reaching the new limit. As a result, the companies requested that the existing capital margins be modified to enable them to continue to expand.
The government recognizes that a number of trust and loan companies are sufficiently sound, financially and from the standpoint of management, to justify some expansion beyond existing limits as previously referred to. In this bill we are, therefore, proposing that the Trust Companies Act and the Loan Companies Act be amended to permit a trust or loan company to borrow-in the case of trust companies it is more accurate to say that they accept money from the public in trust-in excess of 20 times a company's capital and surplus, subject to the adoption of an enabling bylaw establishing a new limit, which bylaw would have to be approved by the minister.
The authority to exceed the limit will also be subject to the ability of the company to meet a number of financial criteria that will be established by regulations. The amendment proposed would also empower the minister to require, as a condition of approving the borrowing bylaw, that some proportion of the additional borrowings in excess of the present limits be in the form of subordinated notes. This is desirable to ensure that a company retains an adequate margin of protection for, first, depositors; second, the holders of guaranteed investment certificates; and third, the holders of ordinary debentures.
As I have mentioned, the issuance of subordinated notes is part and parcel of the increased borrowing limits, and the bill would therefore expand the corporate powers of the companies to enable them to issue such subordinated notes subject to certain limitations designed to avoid confusion between the subordinated notes and any other instrument the company might issue to the public. I should mention here that these notes are intended primarily for sale to institutional investors and will only be issued in denominations of $25,000 or more.
Because of the rapidity. with which events seem to change in the financial world in current years, it is desirable to have some slight flexibility in the application of these limits. Because of rapidly increasing deposits or a drop in security values, a company may find itself at or

near its limits more quickly than might be expected. In order to provide some time to the company to arrange for additional capital or a modification of its pattern of growth, the bill contains two provisions that would, in certain circumstances, permit a company to accept funds in excess of limits otherwise applicable.

It would be expected that the terms and conditions prescribed by the minister would be such as to make the use of subordinated loans in this way a temporary expedient to be replaced by permanent capital at an early date.
It occasionally happens that a company may find itself in excess of the limits imposed by the provisions of the act. Should this happen, the Superintendent of Insurance is required to report to the minister, and the minister may prescribe a time within which the company is to remedy the defect, he may impose conditions on the company or, in an extreme case, he may direct the superintendent to take control of the company's assets.
